# Development of a Functional Beige Fat Cell Line Uncovers Independent Subclasses of Cells Expressing UCP1 and the Futile Creatine Cycle

**Authors:** Ariana Vargas-Castillo; Yizhi Sun; Amanda L. Smythers; Louisa Grauvogel; Phillip A. Dumesic; Margo P. Emont; Linus T. Tsai; Evan D. Rosen; Nathan W Zammit; Sydney Shaffer; Martha Ordonez; Edward T. Chouchani; Steven P. Gygi; Tongtong Wang; Anand Sharma; Miroslav Balaz; Christian Wolfrum; Bruce M. Spiegelman

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Cancer Biology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, MA, USA | 2Department of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | 3Division of Endocrinology, Diabetes and Metabolism, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA, USA | 4Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, Cambridge, MA, USA | 5Department of Immunology, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | 6Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine and the Department of Bioengineering, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA | 7Laboratory of Translational Nutrition Biology, Institute of Food, Nutrition and Health, ETH Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland | 8Laboratory of Cellular and Molecular Metabolism, Biomedical Research Center, Slovak Academy of Sciences, Bratislava, Slovakia | 9Lead contact

## Abstract

While UCP1 is established as a major contributor to adipose thermogenesis, recent data has illustrated an important role for alternative pathways, particularly the Futile Creatine Cycle (FCC). How these pathways co-exist in cells and tissues has not been explored. Beige cell adipogenesis occurs in vivo but has been difficult to model in vitro; here we describe the development of a murine beige cell line that executes a robust respiratory response, including uncoupled respiration and the futile creatine cycle. The key FCC enzyme, TNAP, is localized almost exclusively to mitochondria in these cells. Surprisingly, single cell cloning from this cell line shows that cells with the highest levels of UCP1 express little TNAP, and cells with the highest expression of TNAP express little UCP1. Immunofluorescence analysis of subcutaneous fat from cold exposed mice confirms that the highest levels of these critical thermogenic components are expressed in distinct fat cell populations.

## Abstract

## Abstract

In brief

Different thermogenic mechanisms have been described; how they relate to each other is unknown. Vargas-Castillo et al. developed a beige fat cell line containing both UCP1 and the Futile Creatine Cycle. Clonal and in vivo analyses revealed highest levels of these critical thermogenic components are expressed in distinct fat cell populations.

## INTRODUCTION

Energy expenditure is a major component of the energy balance systems in all animals. In addition to physical activity and basal metabolism, mammals exhibit a process called adaptive thermogenesis whereby energy expenditure can be increased in response to environmental conditions, such as cold, certain diets and key hormones 1. This has profound implications for human disorders of positive energy balance such as obesity and type 2 diabetes 2-4. However, negative energy balance is also a critical component of other serious disorders, such as the cachexia of cancer and cachexia associated with chronic kidney and heart diseases 5,6.

Adaptive thermogenesis is best characterized in adipose tissues. Thermogenic fat, such as brown and beige adipose tissues, has high mitochondrial content and uses those mitochondria to dissipate chemical energy as heat. The most intensively studied tissue is the classical interscapular brown fat of rodents, which expresses high levels of Uncoupling Protein 1 (UCP1) 7. This protein catalyzes a proton leak across the inner mitochondrial membrane, dissipating the electro-chemical gradient formed by the function of the electron transport chain (ETC). This futile cycle of proton movement, fueled by substrate oxidation, achieves no chemical or physical work, thus leading to the release of chemical energy as heat.

More recently, it has been shown that the brown fat-like cells that occur in pockets in the white fat tissues, especially in the subcutaneous fat, are a distinct cell type called beige fat cells 8. These adipocytes do not originate from the Myf5+ skeletal muscle lineage, as does the classical brown fat, but rather arise as a product of a smooth muscle-like cellular lineage 9-11. Adult humans have detectable depots of mitochondrial rich, UCP1+ brown fat; gene expression analyses indicate that most of this tissue more closely resembles murine beige fat, rather than classical brown fat 8,12.

Early studies of UCP1 KO mice indicated that alternative cycles of adaptive thermogenesis must exist. Indeed, hypothermia in these mutant mice exposed to the cold could only be shown in inbred strains. Even a simple F1 cross between two inbred murine strains carrying homozygous mutant UCP1 genes showed little or no hypothermia when exposed to cold temperatures 13. UCP1 KO mice can also adapt to cold temperatures if the decrease in temperature is conducted over days and weeks 14,15. Additionally, white adipose tissue of cold exposed UCP1 KO mice adopts a multilocular lipid droplet morphology similar to that of WT mice 16.

Studies comparing mitochondria of brown and beige fat from cold exposed mice led to the discovery of a new futile, thermogenic cycle termed the Futile Creatine Cycle (FCC) 17. This cycle is a derivative of the classical creatine shuttle by which chemical energy contained within ATP is transferred to creatine through a single phosphorylation event. Phosphocreatine is isoenergetic with ATP and thus is used to phosphorylate ADP when ATP levels are low; the enzymes performing this reaction are called creatine kinases 18. The creatine shuttle is particularly important with tissues having high and variable energetic demands such as heart and skeletal muscle 19,20. The FCC, which is active in beige fat but is also present in brown fat, hydrolyzes phosphocreatine to regenerate creatine and thus cooperates with creatine kinases to dissipate the chemical energy contained initially within ATP generated in the ETC. This futile cycle of phosphocreatine generation and hydrolysis results in the regeneration of ADP, which is required for forward movement of electrons down the ETC 21,22.

Many, if not most cells contain creatine kinases and creatine itself. However thermogenic fat has one highly unusual component: mitochondrial-localized TNAP, a phosphatase capable of hydrolyzing phosphocreatine, a key step to divert energy flow destined to performing work to generating heat 23. TNAP in most cell types is typically secreted or found at the surface of cells expressing it 24. TNAP in brown fat cells localizes to the intermembrane space of mitochondria, where phosphocreatine is produced by mitochondrial creatine kinase. Importantly, inhibition of TNAP in thermogenic fat cells causes a reduction in respiration in culture and in vivo. Fat-selective ablation of TNAP in mice causes early onset obesity with a substantial reduction in energy expenditure 23, highlighting the critical role of this enzyme in the FCC. Since the FCC and UCP1 both dissipate energy contained within mitochondrial membrane potential, these would appear to be competitive pathways; how these pathways co-exist is not clear.

Studying this pathway in beige fat cells has been difficult to model in culture because the development of beige cells in vivo is a “quasi-differentiation” process in response to cold. In lieu of a reliable beige fat cell line, cultured brown fat cells have been used to study the FCC and other beige-enriched pathways 23,25,26. Starting with primary cells from a transgenic murine line with enhanced beige fat development, we have now developed a functional beige cell line which differentiates well and exhibits a robust FCC. Surprisingly, we find that high TNAP and UCP1 levels are contained in distinct cell populations, both in culture and in the beige fat depots in vivo.

## RESULTS

### Generation of a functional beige fat cell line

Various efforts throughout the years have attempted to develop beige cell lines from mice and humans 8,27-29. However, most of these cell lines are difficult to differentiate and/or show little thermogenic function. Here, we have immortalized precursor cells from aP2-Prdm16 transgenic mice, since this model exhibits a robust subcutaneous thermogenic program, even in primary cells 30. We isolated the SVF from the inguinal white adipose tissue (iWAT) of aP2-Prdm16 mice and their WT littermate controls. As expected, flow cytometry demonstrated more PDGFRα+/SCA1+ beige adipocyte precursor cells within SVF of aP2-Prdm16 mice (Figure S1A). We immortalized all SVF-derived cells using retrovirus encoding Large T antigen from SV40 virus. After reaching 20 passages, we differentiated these non-clonal cell lines to adipocytes and evaluated their thermogenic capacity through gene expression and respirometry. Importantly, both cell lines have a very high adipogenic capacity upon differentiation (Figure 1A), with greater than 90% of cells showing a rounded morphology with multiple lipid droplets. As shown in Figure 1B, the SV40-Prdm16 cell line (beige cell line) shows robust respiration in response to forskolin stimulation, which increases both total respiration and proton leak-related respiration (uncoupled respiration) (Figure 1B and S1B). The control SV40-WT cells also respire more upon forskolin stimulation but with a far smaller magnitude. Next, we analyzed the expression of thermogenic genes after increasing cAMP levels through stimulation with the phosphodiesterase inhibitor, 3-isobutyl-1-methylxanthine (IBMX). The SV40-Prdm16 adipocytes show higher expression of classical thermogenic genes, including Ucp1, Pgc1α, Dio2, and Cidea. Importantly, these cells also show elevated expression of Alpl (encoding TNAP), a key gene involved in the Futile Creatine Cycle (FCC) (Figure 1C). Ckb is also induced, but in this case the SV40-WT cell line has more Ckb expression than the SV40-Prdm16 cell line. Mitochondrial creatine kinases, Ckmt1 and Ckmt2 are induced in SV40-Prdm16 cells, although Ckb is more abundant in absolute levels. Genes involved in calcium cycling did not increase upon stimulation; some genes potentially involved in lipid cycling are slightly increased even at basal levels in the SV40-Prdm16 cells (Figure S1C). Absolute Ucp1 gene expression is decreased in immortalized cells compared to primary cells (Figure S1D): the SV40-Prdm16 cells express roughly half the amount of Ucp1 as that observed in iWAT primary cells. However, this amount is enough to contribute to robust respiration upon stimulation. Interestingly, Alpl absolute levels were not decreased, but rather increased as compared to primary cells. The expression of other adipogenic and thermogenic genes can be found in Figure S1E. Thus, the SV40-Prdm16 cells appear to exhibit much of the beige adipose phenotype after immortalization.

### SV40-Prdm16 adipocytes run an active futile creatine cycle

As shown in Figure 2A, the SV40-Prdm16 cells have elevated levels of both UCP1 and TNAP within their mitochondria, compared to the control cells. It was critical then to ask whether SV40-Prdm16 cells can run a functional FCC. For that purpose, we treated the cells overnight with beta-guanidinopropionic acid (β-GPA), a creatine analogue that inhibits creatine transport into cells 31. SV40-Prdm16 cells pretreated with β-GPA had 30% less forskolin-stimulated oxygen consumption rate (OCR) compared to vehicle, but no significant difference in maximal respiration (Figure 2B). In contrast, SV40-WT cells did not change their OCR upon β-GPA treatment (Figure S2A). Another strategy to examine the FCC is through treatment with the highly specific TNAP inhibitor SBI-425 32. After an acute treatment, SV40-Prdm16 cells display reduced forskolin-stimulated respiration, in a concentration dependent manner and without changes in the maximal respiration (Figure 2B). Again, the control SV40-WT cells do not show changes in OCR after SBI-425 treatment (Figure S2A). In addition to whole cell respiration, we assessed whether the FCC is active in the mitochondria of SV40-Prdm16 adipocytes. Kazak et al. have shown that creatine will drive the regeneration of a super-stoichiometric quantity of ADP, resulting in a surplus of oxygen consumption under ADP-limiting conditions 17,25. As shown in Figure 2C, mitochondria isolated from SV40-Prdm16 cells respire more when creatine is present and ADP concentrations are limiting. Overall, the results indicate that SV40-Prdm16 cells express an active FCC.

### Clonal analysis reveals at least two subclasses of thermogenic adipocytes, a UCP1+ population and an FCC population

Following the characterization of the SV40-Prdm16 beige cell line, we studied clonal cell lines generated through limiting dilution of the parental line. In total, 96 of the 100 clones generated were adipogenic and these were further tested with IBMX stimulation. While some of these clonal lines expressed moderate levels of both Ucp1 and Alpl mRNAs, it was striking that clones with the highest Ucp1 gene expression, like clones #67, #90, #91, #99 and #59, had very little Alpl expression (Figure 3A). Conversely, multiple clones with the highest Alpl gene expression, like #37, #20, #40, #44 and #79, expressed relatively low levels of Ucp1 mRNA. Overall, the correlation between Ucp1 and Alpl mRNAs was low, with a p value=0.07 and a correlation coefficient r=0.18. Using immunocytochemistry, we could visualize adipocyte heterogeneity in the SV40-Prdm16 parental cell line: some cells were TNAP-enriched (Alpl-dominant) and other cells UCP1-enriched (Ucp1-dominant) (Figure S3A).

We selected several of these clones and measured their mitochondrial protein expression (Figure 3B). Clones with high Alpl gene expression also have more TNAP protein in mitochondrial extracts and high Ucp1 gene expression clones have more UCP1 protein (Figure 3B). In addition, we confirmed by immunocytochemistry that clone #37, an Alpl-dominant clone, has higher TNAP protein abundance than does the Ucp1-dominant clone #59, which contains more UCP1 protein (Figure 3C).

To determine whether these clones have a functional FCC, we treated both types of clonal cells with the specific TNAP inhibitor SBI-425. Alpl-dominant clones, for instance #37 and #79, have reduced forskolin-stimulated respiration after acute SBI-425 treatment (Figure 3D), suggesting an active FCC. In contrast, Ucp1-dominant clones such as #59 and #67 did not change their respiration upon SBI-425 treatment (Figure 3D). We tested additional Alpl-dominant and Ucp1-dominant clones and they presented similar behavior (Figure S3B). It is worth noting that certain other clones that showed high Alpl or Ucp1 expression did not have a functional FCC phenotype or total respiration was poor (Figure S3C).

### UCP1high adipocytes and TNAPhigh adipocytes are identified in different cell populations in vivo after cold exposure

Our results in vitro show that the highest Ucp1 and Alpl expression reside in different cell populations. Therefore, it was critical to determine whether these results were representative of beige cells in vivo. We thus used immunofluorescence to examine TNAP (encoded by the Alpl gene) or UCP1 proteins in the iWAT of WT mice exposed to the cold for two weeks. Additionally, we stained the mitochondrial marker HSP60 to distinguish mitochondrial TNAP from TNAP in other cellular locations. Importantly, as shown in Figure 4A, TNAP in the inguinal fat depot was found almost exclusively in the mitochondria, since TNAP and HSP60 signals overlap 86% (Figure 4B), as quantitated by CellProfiler 33. We also confirmed the specificity of the TNAP signal using Adipo-Alpl KO mice (Figure 4A), an adipose TNAP-deficient animal model 23. As shown in Figure S4A, we can identify three areas of the iWAT: the dorsolumbar (DL), lymph node (LN) and inguinal (ING) areas. In those three areas, using perilipin as an adipocyte identity marker, we identified adipocytes expressing TNAP and UCP1. Of all three areas the lymph node area and inguinal area show the most thermogenic regions (Figure S4B-C). In particular, we identified regions with a robust TNAP and much less UCP1 expression (TNAPhi/UCP1low). In addition, other areas were identified containing adipocytes expressing mostly UCP1 and much less TNAP (UCP1hi/ TNAPlow). It is important to note that some areas showed adipocytes expressing both UCP1 and mitochondrial TNAP (TNAPhi/UCP1hi) (Figure 4C). Quantitative cell segmentation analysis and fluorescence quantification by Cellpose and Cellprofiler, on average indicated that adipocytes expressing mainly mitochondrial TNAP (TNAPhi/UCP1low) represent approximately more than one quarter of the adipocytes (~27%) (Figure 4D). Moreover, adipocytes expressing mainly UCP1 (UCP1hi/ TNAPlow) represent around one fifth (~22%) of the adipocytes; adipocytes expressing comparable amount of UCP1 and mitochondrial TNAP (TNAPhi/UCP1hi) represent around half of the cells (51%). Consistent with what we found in our cell clones, some adipocyte populations in vivo preferentially express UCP1, while other beige cell populations preferentially express mitochondrial TNAP.

The next question was to identify whether any of these adipocyte populations exist in human fat. In human deep neck brown fat biopsies, we co-stained TNAP, UCP1 and COX4, a mitochondrial marker. Interestingly, we readily detected a TNAP-enriched adipocyte population (Figure 4E). Fluorescence profile analysis show that the TNAP signals coincide with COX4 signals, suggesting mitochondrial TNAP localization (Figure S4D). In contrast, UCP1 signal was very low, perhaps due to the origin of the samples which were taken from humans at basal conditions, without an external thermogenic stimulation. These findings suggests that the futile creatine cycle might be relevant in human fat bioenergetics. However, more experiments in humans will be required to corroborate and extend these findings.

## DISCUSSION

Adaptive thermogenesis in adipose tissues is a major contributor to whole body energy expenditure, at least in rodents. Humans clearly have thermogenic “brown” fat 34-36, though its overall importance in physiology is not completely understood37-39. Rodent thermogenic fat contains at least two classes of cells. One class, epitomized by the interscapular brown fat, has a high mitochondrial content and expresses copious amounts of UCP1. This protein, which is selectively expressed in thermogenic fat, uncouples fuel oxidation from ATP synthesis by catalyzing proton leak across the inner mitochondrial membrane. A second class of thermogenic fat cells is called beige fat; these cells, also rich in mitochondria, emerge in white fat depots upon chronic exposure of rodents to cold or certain hormones. These cells arise from a completely different cell lineage than the classical brown fat 8,10,30. Importantly, much of human “brown fat” is composed of cells that have a gene signature that is closer to rodent beige fat than the classical brown fat 8,12. The similarity and differences in function between brown and beige fat cells remains under intensive study.

While cultured murine primary brown fat cells are a very useful system to study classical brown fat, no convenient and reliable cellular system exists for the study of beige fat. Beige fat arises, at least in part, from a differentiation in vivo that is difficult to replicate in culture. Immortalized inguinal preadipocyte cells from rodents behave as white fat cells upon differentiation, with limited thermogenic capacity. An immortalized human beige fat cell system has been described 28 , but the differentiation of these cells is a lengthy process and often incomplete.

We have now created a robustly functional beige cell line by taking advantage of a transgenic mouse that has elevated expression of the transcriptional coregulator Prdm16. Prdm16 is clearly a dominant factor in the development of beige fat tissues in vivo. Transgenic mice overexpressing Prdm16 in adipose tissues have greatly enhanced beige fat, even at room temperature, with no observable changes in the interscapular brown fat 30. The critical role of this factor is also observed in mice lacking Prdm16 in adipose tissues; these mice have almost no beige fat, even upon cold exposure. Again, the brown fat was quite normal 40,41. In this paper, we demonstrate that immortalized inguinal fat cells from this transgenic mouse strain retain a high and hormone-inducible capacity for mitochondrial respiration, unlike immortalized cells from control (non-transgenic) mice. These cells grow well in culture and differentiate almost completely within 8 days. Most importantly, these cells express elevated levels of both Ucp1 and Alpl, a critical gene of the FCC. TNAP, encoded by the Alpl gene, is largely incorporated into mitochondria of thermogenic fat cells 23. In fact, mitochondrial TNAP is likely the only component of the FCC that has not been found in other cell types, as creatine kinases and creatine itself are found in most mammalian cell types, at some measurable level. Lastly, the SV40-Prdm16 cells run a substantial FCC, as evidenced by the fact that stimulated respiration in these cells is reduced by two chemical treatments that inhibit the FCC, and by a super-stoichiometric increase in mitochondrial respiration when creatine is added under ADP limiting concentrations.

Clonal analysis of these immortalized cells gave an unexpected insight into how UCP1 can co-exist with the FCC. These pathways both dissipate the chemical energy contained within the mitochondrial membrane potential, so they would appear to compete with each other and make each pathway less effective. While some clonal cells express both Ucp1 and Alpl RNAs at moderate levels, cells with the highest levels of Ucp1 and Alpl mRNAs show relatively low levels of the other. Moreover, cells with the highest UCP1 levels demonstrate essentially no FCC upon respiratory analysis. Importantly, immunofluorescence analyses of murine adipose tissues exposed to the cold also demonstrate that high mitochondrial TNAP and high UCP1 protein levels exist in distinct adipocytes; both subclasses together constitute approximately half of the beige cell population. The other half consists of adipocytes expressing both TNAP and UCP1. This finding aligns with the reported heterogeneity in beige adipocytes regarding UCP1 expression 42. These data together also emphasize that the expression of UCP1 should not be used as a sole determinant of whether fat cells in mice or humans are thermogenic. We detected adipocytes corresponding to the high mitochondrial TNAP population in human deep neck brown fat tissue, suggesting an important role of the FCC in human fat physiology and bioenergetics.

The cell lines developed here, both parental and clonal, should allow a detailed analysis of the FCC and other outstanding questions. These include how TNAP in beige cells is incorporated into mitochondria, in the apparent absence of a mitochondrial targeting sequence 23. These cells should also allow a discrimination of the transcriptional basis for development of these two subclasses of beige cells, as well as the identification of signaling events that are associated with different thermogenic pathways 43. Of course, it seems likely that further classes of beige fat cells, including “g-beige cells” 44, might also be contained within these immortalized cell populations.

### Limitations of study

We generated a beige fat cell line through the immortalization of adipose precursors of aP2-Prdm16 transgenic mice. However, we note that after the immortalization process, continuous passage likely selected for cells with high proliferation capacity, both in parental and clonal cell lines. This means that we may not have captured the full heterogeneity of beige adipocytes. In this paper, we quantified the abundance of each adipocyte subclass in inguinal fat tissue, in particular in sections corresponding to the core of the tissue. Therefore, percentages might change outside the core. Moreover, percentages might be different in other fat depots. At present, we have not identified specific cell surface polypeptides that enable isolation of each population directly from the fat tissues. More experiments in human fat samples can also help reveal the most prevalent thermogenic beige fat populations and how these might be affected during metabolic diseases.

### EXPERIMENTAL MODEL AND SUBJECT DETAILS

#### Animals

All animal experiments were performed according to protocols approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC). All mice were housed at 22°C under a 12 h light/dark cycle, with free access to food and water. Male mice 6-8 weeks old were used for all animal experiments. For the immortalized cell lines, we extracted the adipose precursors from the aP2-Prdm16 transgenic mice 30, along with WT littermates. For the immunofluorescence experiments, aP2-Prdm16 mice and Adipo-Alpl KO mice 23 were used with their WT littermates.

#### Human fat biopsies

The clinical study was reviewed and approved by the Local Ethics Committee of the University Hospital in Bratislava, Slovakia. All study participants provided witnessed written informed consent prior entering the study. Deep neck BAT samples were obtained as described before 45. In brief, samples were obtained from the lower third of the neck by an experienced ENT surgeon during neck surgery under general anesthesia. The deep neck adipose tissue sample was taken from pre- and paravertebral space between common carotid and trachea. Patients with malignant disease and subjects younger than 18 years were excluded from participation in the study. Adipose tissue samples of 3 patients undergoing thyroid surgery (Females, 53.5 ± 3.3 years; BMI 27.8 ± 1.9 kg/m2; body fat 35.3 ± 2.7 %) were immediately cleaned from blood and connective tissue in ice-cold saline, fixed in formalin and embedded in paraffin. Tissue was sectioned at a thickness of 5 μm.

### METHOD DETAILS

#### Primary adipocyte isolation

The stromal vascular fraction (SVF) of inguinal White Adipose Tissue (iWAT) was isolated from 6-8 week old male mice. Inguinal WAT was dissected, washed in PBS, minced, and digested for 45 minutes at 37°C in PBS containing 10 mg ml−1 collagenase D (Roche), 3 U ml−1 Dispase II (Roche), and 10 mM CaCl2. The cell suspension was then combined with adipocyte culture medium (DMEM/F12 supplemented with GlutaMAX [1:1, Invitrogen], 10% fetal bovine serum [GeminiBio] and 100 U ml−1 Penicillin [Gibco], 100 μg ml−1 Streptomycin [Gibco]) and filtered through a 100 μm cell strainer. SVF cells were pelleted by centrifugation at 600g for 5 min. The cell pellet was resuspended in adipocyte culture medium, filtered through a 40 μm cell strainer and pelleted by centrifugation at 600g for 5 min. Cell pellet was resuspended and plated in adipocyte culture medium. Cells were cultured at 37°C with 10% CO2.

### Generation of immortalized fat cell lines

Before primary cells infection, we generated retroviral particles using the cell line Phoenix-ECO (ATCC). These cells were transfected with 10 μg of retroviral plasmid pBABE-puro SV40 LT (Addgene no. 13970 46) DNA using Lipofectamine 2000 DNA Transfection Reagent (Invitrogen). Media-containing virus was collected and refreshed every 24 h until 72 h after transfection. Media was filtered through a 0.45 μm filter. Primary preadipocytes from aP2-Prdm16 and WT littermates were seeded in 6-well plates until reaching 60-70% confluence, then were infected with media containing pBABE-SV40 LT virus diluted 1:3 in adipocyte culture medium in the presence of 4 μg/ml Polybrene. 24 h after infection, media containing SV40 LT virus was removed and replaced with regular adipocyte culture medium. The next day, cells were passaged and plated into 10 cm dishes. A control of primary cells exposed to media without virus allowed us to detect when primary cells normally stop dividing (around passage 7). Cells were continuously passaged 20 times, every time reaching 60-70% confluence. Following this strategy, we avoided antibiotic selection, allowing us to preserve a healthy functionality, as much as possible.

### Culture and differentiation of immortalized fat cell lines

SV40-Prdm16 and SV40-WT cell lines were grown to 100% confluency. The next day cells were exposed to differentiation media for 4 days, refreshing the media on day 2. Differentiation media is the adipocyte culture medium as described above containing an adipogenic cocktail of 0.5 mM isobutylmethylxanthine [IBMX] (Sigma), 5 μM dexamethasone (Sigma), 1 μM rosiglitazone (Cayman Chemical), 1 nM 3,3’,5-triiodo-L-thyronine [T3] (Sigma) and 850 nM insulin (Sigma). The next 4 days of differentiation, cells were exposed to maintenance media, consisting of adipocyte culture medium and 850 nM insulin, refreshing the media every other day. On day 8 post-induction, cells are fully mature. To stimulate thermogenesis, cells were treated 4 h with 0.5 mM IBMX, for gene expression analysis. For protein expression studies, cells were treated 12 h with 0.5 mM IBMX.

### Generation of immortalized clonal cell lines

Single cell clones were obtained from the SV40-Prdm16 parental cell line by limiting dilution of cells into 96-well plates (0.2 cells/well). Wells containing proliferating cells were trypsinized and further propagated in 48-well, 24-well, 12-well, 6-well plates and finally 10 cm dishes. A total of 100 clonal cell lines originated from the parental SV40-Prdm16 cells were screened for adipogenic potential. In total, 96 of 100 clones were adipogenic and were stimulated with 0.5 mM IBMX for 4 h to test their thermogenic capacity. Clones #37 and #79 were selected as Alpl-dominant cell lines and clones #59 and #67 as Ucp1-dominant clones for further analysis.

### Cellular Respiration Assays

Cellular respiration of both parental and clonal cell lines was measured using an XF24 Extracellular Flux Analyzer (Seahorse Bioscience). Cells were differentiated as described above in 6-well plates. On day 3, cells were trypsinized, counted and plated at 14,000 cells per well of an XF24 V7 cell culture microplates. Differentiation continued as described above until day 8. On day 8 of differentiation, the adipocyte culture medium was changed to respiration medium consisting of DMEM lacking NaHCO3 (Sigma), 1.85 g l−1 NaCl (ThermoFisher), 25 mM glucose (Sigma), 2% fatty-acid-free BSA (Roche), and 1 mM sodium pyruvate (ThermoFisher) at pH 7.4.

Cells followed the Mito Stress Test (Seahorse Bioscience) to measure the oxygen consumption rate (OCR). For SV40-Prdm16 and SV-40 WT parental cell lines, cells were treated with 10 μM Forskolin to stimulate acute respiration, followed by 5 μM oligomycin to inhibit coupled respiration. Maximal respiration was determined by addition of 5 μM carbonyl cyanide m-chlorophenylhydrazone (CCCP), followed by 5 μM Rotenone and 5 μM Antimycin A to inhibit mitochondrial respiration. For uncoupled respiration, we followed the injection strategy as previously described 47. For FCC functional evaluation, before the experiment cells were treated either i) overnight with 2 mM beta-guanidinopropionic acid (β-GPA) or vehicle (water) ii) or 1 h before the experiment with 33 μM and 100 μM SBI-425 (specific TNAP inhibitor) or vehicle (DMSO). Both inhibitors of FCC were supplemented in final respiration buffer. For selected clonal cell lines cellular respiration evaluation, cells were treated acutely with 33 μM SBI-425 in Port A and after 30 min, Forskolin was injected. Then, Rotenone/Antimycin A were injected to block mitochondrial respiration. For parameters quantification, we followed equations recommended from Agilent Seahorse to calculate basal respiration, proton leak, maximal respiration and non-mitochondrial respiration. Wave v.2.6 software was used for data collection.

### mRNA expression analysis

Total RNA was extracted from cells using TRIzol (Invitrogen) and RNeasy Mini purification kit (Qiagen), and reverse transcribed using a HighCapacity cDNA Reverse Transcription kit (Applied Biosystems). The resultant cDNA was analyzed by quantitative PCR using SYBR green fluorescent dye 2x qPCR master mix (Promega) in a QuantStudio 6 Flex Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems). For all gene expression experiments, Tbp mRNA was used as a housekeeping gene, and relative expression was calculated using the ΔΔCt method, relative to the SV40-WT cell line treated with vehicle (DMSO). For absolute values graphs, we calculated 2^-ΔCt*1000. Primer sequences for mouse and human can be found in Table S1.

### Mitochondria isolation

For western blot of mitochondria lysates, we isolated mitochondria following the protocol described previously 23. The whole procedure was conducted at 4°C. Differentiated cells from parental and clonal cell lines were grown in 15 cm dishes. On day 8, cells were scraped gently using ice-cold SHE buffer (250 mM sucrose, 10 mM HEPES, 0.1 mM EGTA, 0.1% fatty acid-free BSA [Roche] and 1x EDTA-free Protease Inhibitor Cocktail [Roche], pH 7.2) and further homogenized with a motorized Teflon pestle.

Homogenates were spun at 8,500g for 10 min and the fat layer was discarded. The pellet was resuspended in SHE buffer and spun at 600g for 10 min to spin down nuclei and cell debris. The supernatant was spun at 8,500g for 10 min to pellet mitochondria. Mitochondrial pellet was washed with SHE buffer [without BSA] twice and protein was quantified using BCA Protein Assay Kits (Pierce).

For respiration analysis, we followed the methodology described previously 25. The whole procedure was conducted at 4°C. SV40-Prdm16 differentiated adipocytes grown in 15 cm dishes were scraped gently using ice-cold hypotonic buffer (20 mM HEPES, pH 7.8; 5 mM KCl; 1.5 mM MgCl2; 0.1% fatty-acid-free BSA). Cells were homogenized in a tight-fitting dounce homogenizer with 25 strokes, and equilibrated to a 1x MSH buffer (210 mM mannitol; 70 mM sucrose; 20 mM HEPES, pH 7.8) using a 2.5x MSH stock. The homogenate was spun at 8,500g for 10 min and the fat layer was discarded. The pellet was resuspended in 1x MSH buffer and spun at 600g for 5 min to spin down nuclei and cell debris. The supernatant was spun at 8,500g for 10 min to pellet mitochondria. Mitochondria were resuspended in MSH buffer and protein was quantified using BCA Protein Assay Kits (Pierce).

### Mitochondria respiration

An XF24 Extracellular Flux Analyzer (Seahorse Bioscience) was used to determine mitochondrial respiration as previously described 23. Briefly, 15 μg mitochondria isolated from SV40-Prdm16 differentiated adipocytes were plated in each well of the XF24 V7 cell culture microplate, in a cold respiration buffer (125 mM sucrose, 20 mM K-TES at pH 7.2, 2 mM MgCl2, 1 mM EDTA, 4 mM KH2PO4, 0.1% fatty-acid-free BSA, 10 mM pyruvate, 5 mM malate and 1 mM GDP); and adhered to the bottom by centrifugation at 2,000g for 20 min at 4°C. Pilot experiments titrating ADP concentrations were conducted to determine the limiting ADP concentration for the mitochondria isolated from SV40-Prdm16 adipocytes (0.3 mM ADP). Then, some wells were treated with 0.01 mM creatine or vehicle (water) and coupled respiration was initiated by addition of 0.3 mM of ADP to detect the creatine-dependent stimulation. Rotenone and Antimycin A (10 μM each) were used to inhibit Complex 1- and Complex 3-dependent respiration.

### Flow cytometry

Fat depots from WT and aP2-Prdm16 mice were processed for flow cytometry following the method previously described48. In brief, eWAT, iWAT and BAT were harvested, placed into Dulbelcco’s Modified Eagle’s Medium (DMEM) containing 2% fetal bovine serum (FBS), minced to disaggregate the tissue, and incubated with 1.5 mg/ml Collagenase type II (Sigma) at 37°C for 20 minutes. For flow cytometry, cell preparations were subjected to red blood cell lysis. Cells were stained with antibodies recognizing CD45 (#103125), CD31 (#102406), SCA1 (#108124), and PDGFRα (#135908) (BioLegend). Incubations were done for ~20 minutes at 4°C.

### Western blot

Mitochondria was isolated as described above. After protein quantification, mitochondria protein samples were denatured in 1x NuPAGE LDS Sample Buffer (Invitrogen) without boiling, resolved by 4-12% NuPAGE Bis-Tris gels (Invitrogen), and transferred to polyvinylidene difluoride membrane with 0.45 μm pore size (Immobilon-P). Membranes were blocked with Tris-buffered saline with 0.05% Tween-20 (TBST) containing 5% dried nonfat milk (Biorad), and were incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibody diluted in TBST containing 5% dried nonfat milk. For secondary antibody incubation, membranes were incubated for 1 h at room temperature with anti-rabbit HRP (Promega) or anti-goat HRP (Promega) diluted in TBST containing 5% dried nonfat milk. Secondary antibodies were visualized using Immobilon Crescendo Western HRP substrate (Millipore). Primary antibodies were used to detect: TNAP (AF2910, R&D Systems), UCP1 (ab10983, Abcam), HSP60 (12165, Cell Signaling), TOMM20 (42406S, Cell Signaling) and Actin (4967S, Cell signaling).

### Immunofluorescent imaging and analysis

Inguinal adipose tissues from 2-week cold exposed mice were excised, fixed overnight in 4% formalin, then were dehydrated in alcohol, cleared in xylenes and embedded in paraffin. iWAT was sectioned by the Rodent Histopathology Core at Dana-Farber/Harvard Cancer Center at a thickness of 5 μm. For immunostaining, we selected sections from the core of the tissue. For unwaxing, antigen retrieval and following steps, we followed the methodology previously described 49. Antigen retrieval was done using citrate buffer, pH: 6.0 (C9999, Sigma). Slides were washed 3 times with PBS, and blocked by blocking solution (PBS supplemented with 0.1% Triton X-100, 1% BSA and 2% donkey serum) for 1 h at room temperature. Sections were incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies previously diluted in blocking solution. For mouse tissue slides we used: anti-TNAP goat antibody 1:20 (AF2910, R&D Systems), anti-UCP1 rabbit antibody 1:200 (ab10983, Abcam), anti-HSP60 mouse antibody 1:50 (MA3-012, Invitrogen). Another set of slides were stained with anti-perilipin mouse antibody 1:200 (MA5-27861, Invitrogen), TNAP and UCP1 antibodies, as described above. Sections were washed 3 times with PBS and stained with anti-goat Alexa Fluor 488 (A11055, Invitrogen), anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor 568 (A10042, Invitrogen) and anti-mouse Alexa Fluor 647 (A31571, Invitrogen) secondary antibody at room temperature for 1 h. Sections were washed 3 times with PBS and coverslips were mounted in ProLong Diamond Antifade Mountant (Invitrogen). For immunocytochemistry, SV40-Prdm16 parental cell line, clone #37 and clone #59 were grown and differentiated in 8-well chamber slides. At the end of differentiation, cells were treated with 0.5mM IBMX for 12 h. Then, were fixed in fresh 4% paraformaldehyde (Electron Microscopy Sciences) in PBS at pH of 7.4 for 15 min at 4°C, followed by 3 washes with PBS. Blocking steps and antibody incubations are the same as described above. For human paraffin-embedded slides, we used: anti-TNAP rat antibody 1:25 (MAB29091, R&D Systems), anti-UCP1 rabbit antibody 1:200 (ab155117, Abcam), anti-COX4-I1 goat antibody 1:50 (AF5814, R&D Systems). For secondary antibodies: anti-rat Alexa Fluor 488 (A21208, Invitrogen), anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor 568 (A10042, Invitrogen) and anti-goat Alexa Fluor 647 (A21447, Invitrogen). All fluorescent images for full tissue scans were acquired at DFCI Molecular Imaging Core using LASX Office 1.4.5 27713 on a Leica THUNDER Imager wide-field microscope. A Zeiss 980 Confocal/Spectral/Airyscan microscope was used for closer images, using Zen 3.7 microscopy software for image processing and profile quantification. Images were managed using Fiji 50. For HSP60 and TNAP colocalization analysis, a total of 250 images were made into masks using CellProfiler 33. The segmented masks and original images were then fed into CellProfiler to calculate the correlation overlap between TNAP and HSP60. For quantification of the different cell populations, a total of 84 photos were segmented using Cellpose 51 (cell diameter: 450 pixels, channel to segment: grey (Perilipin), flow_threshold: 0.6, model zoo: cyto2). Each photo was made into masks and analyzed using CellProfiler. In total, 3369 cells were quantified. Each fluorescence signal was normalized to the maximal value of its channel. Perilipin+ cells with low intensity values for both proteins were excluded from the quantification. A fluorescence ratio was calculated per cell (TNAP signal/UCP1 signal). Rangs were defined, when the ratio is below ≤0.75 corresponds to UCP1hi/TNAPlow, >0.75 and <1.5 corresponds to TNAPhi/UCP1hi population, and ≥1.5 corresponds to TNAPhi/UCP1low population.

### Statistical analyses

All data are represented as mean ± S.E.M. Significance was considered as p<0.05. P-values were calculated using either two-tailed unpaired t-test for pairwise comparison of variables, one-way ANOVA for multiple comparison of variables, and two-way ANOVA for multiple comparisons involving two independent variables. For cellular assays, n corresponds to the number of experimental replicates. For animal assays, n corresponds to the number of mice used per genotype or condition. All used statistical tests and n numbers are presented in figure legends. For cold exposure studies, mice were randomly assigned to groups. Sample sizes were determined on the basis of previous experiments using similar methodologies. All experiments were repeated with similar results at least three times. Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism 7. Figures were generated using GraphPad Prism 7, Adobe Illustrator, and BioRender.com
